extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, patent attorneys/agents, and USPTO disciplinary stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and sanctions applied by the USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline for practitioner misconduct involving client communication, timely filing, and related duties under the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely filing to preserve provisional priority
rubrics_metrics.description: The client's nonprovisional patent application claiming priority to the provisional application had to be filed not later than 12 months after the date on which the provisional application was filed (i.e., by January 16, 2008).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to file the nonprovisional within 12 months causes the client to lose priority to the provisional application and the benefit of the provisional application's filing date; practitioners must calendar and track such deadlines and ensure filings that preserve priority when instructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate / keep client reasonably informed
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner in a practitioner-client relationship owes the clients fiduciary duties including the duty to communicate with the clients in order to keep them reasonably informed about the status of their cases so that they can make informed decisions about the direction of the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The duty to communicate reasonably includes a duty of care to ascertain if the actions the practitioner intends to take on behalf of the clients accurately reflect the clients' desires. A failure to communicate will result in a practitioner's violation of the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility or the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to seek the client's lawful objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(1) concerns intentionally failing to seek the lawful objectives of the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must act to pursue the legitimate goals the client has instructed them to pursue (e.g., preserving priority when the client expects it); intentional failure to do so constitutes professional misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to carry out a contract of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(2) concerns failing to carry out a contract of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When retained to perform specified services (for example, to draft and file a nonprovisional application claiming priority), practitioners must perform those services as contracted or obtain client agreement before deviating; failing to carry out agreed work can constitute misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to avoid causing prejudice or damage to the client
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(3) concerns causing prejudice or damage to the client (here, by not filing a nonprovisional application and a PCT application within one year of the provisional priority date after being instructed to do so, and not discussing such action with the client before taking it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must not take actions (or omissions) that foreseeably prejudice the client's rights; failing to meet critical deadlines or failing to consult before disadvantaging decisions are examples of conduct causing prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to obtain client consultation/authority before substantive filing changes
rubrics_metrics.description: At no time did Respondent consult with his client in advance of editing and filing the nonprovisional application and PCT application; Respondent removed priority claims without client consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before altering substantive aspects of an application that affect the client's rights (e.g., removing claims to priority), a practitioner should consult the client and obtain authority; unilateral substantive changes that adversely affect rights are improper and can be disciplinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating/aggravating factors affecting discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent has expressed remorse and is cooperating; Respondent has no prior disciplinary history. Nothing in the Final Order prevents the Office from considering the record of this proceeding in future matters as an aggravating factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remorse, cooperation, and lack of prior discipline can mitigate sanction; however, the record may be used later to aggravate discipline or rebut representations in subsequent proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and public notice for practitioner misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreed upon sanction: Respondent is publicly reprimanded; the OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at OED's FOIA Reading Room and publish notice in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary outcomes include public reprimand and publication of the decision; publication serves notice to the public and may factor into future disciplinary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO jurisdiction and governing rules for practitioner discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction over this matter pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32, and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19 and 11.26. The events occurred before May 3, 2013, so the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility applies (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.20 through 10.112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be aware of the statutory and regulatory bases for discipline and which version of the USPTO professional conduct rules applies to the conduct at issue; different rule sets may apply depending on the date of the events.
